title: BCCI Faces Medical Staff Crisis as Injury Woes Mount for Indian Cricket
excerpt: Former India batter Mohammed Kaif questions why the richest cricket board struggles to attract top medical professionals, as communication gaps between Centre of Excellence and team management come under scrutiny.
body:
• BCCI has not appointed a new head of medical staff and 2023 SOPs remain unrevised
  • Reports indicate players were fielded before being fully fit, contributing to a string of hamstring injuries
  • Communication breakdown between Centre of Excellence in Bengaluru and team management is under scrutiny
  • Former India batter Mohammed Kaif questioned why the world's richest cricket board struggles to hire top medical experts

The Board of Control for Cricket in India is grappling with a medical staffing crisis that former India batter Mohammed Kaif has called "surprising" for an organisation with the financial resources of the BCCI.

A detailed report by The Times of India has exposed significant communication failures between the BCCI's Centre of Excellence (CoE) in Bengaluru and the Indian team management, contributing to a wave of injuries that has disrupted India's international campaigns.

"Several hamstring injuries suggest that the players were put on the field despite not being fully fit. There seems to be a lack of communication between the CoE and the team management about the players and fitness."

— BCCI official

Players Cleared Before Full Recovery

The report highlighted specific cases that have raised alarm bells within Indian cricket. Nitish Kumar Reddy's bowling workload management was flagged as a concern, with sources noting that his efforts to increase pace with England bowling coach Stephen Jones should have been a more gradual process.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=ohM-k8jRtMM

More worrying was the revelation about all-rounder Harshit Rana. According to the report, the CoE cleared Harshit for selection at the team management's behest, even though he had not regained the weight he carried before his knee injury — a key indicator of full recovery.

"It is worrisome that at the behest of the team management, the CoE cleared Harshit, even though he did not return the weight he had before the knee injury. These things need to be addressed," the BCCI source stated.

Structural Problems at the CoE

Since the departure of former head physiotherapist Nitin Patel, the Centre of Excellence has been operating with a relatively small medical team. The BCCI has yet to announce a replacement for the head of medical staff position, and Standard Operating Procedures drafted in 2023 have not been updated to reflect current requirements.

The lack of a centralised injury management system has led to situations where players are managing their own recovery. During IPL 2026, Mumbai Indians captain Rohit Sharma was forced to personally contact the BCCI database to access his own injury history after the franchise management failed to identify a hamstring problem.

Kaif Questions BCCI's Priorities

Kaif, who has been vocal about Indian cricket's fitness management on his YouTube channel, questioned why top medical professionals are declining contracts with the CoE despite the BCCI's considerable financial muscle.

The former middle-order batsman pointed out that India's key players — Virat Kohli, Rohit Sharma and Jasprit Bumrah — all need carefully managed workloads, and the current medical infrastructure appears inadequate for that task.

Impact on Upcoming Assignments

India face a demanding international schedule, including Test series against Sri Lanka, New Zealand and Australia within the current World Test Championship cycle. Captain Shubman Gill recently underlined the importance of workload management after India's ODI series defeat to England, acknowledging that the team cannot afford to keep losing key players to preventable injuries.

The BCCI is expected to conduct a thorough review of the team's medical and support staff setup, but whether substantive changes will follow remains to be seen. For a board that earned over ₹15,000 crore in its most recent media rights cycle, the inability to attract and retain world-class medical professionals represents an institutional failure that extends well beyond the cricket field.
